RX Radio: Broadcasting for Children by Children

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We hear the young voices behind the microphone of the first radio station in the world to live-stream from a children’s hospital: presented by children they share their life stories.

Unique Selling Point:
RX Radio at the Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital in Cape Town is presented by children who share their stories of hope and understanding their chronic health conditions they live with. Talking about their experiences in hospital helps them to cope better and teaches them valuable life skills.


Summary:
The Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital is dedicated entirely to children. The hospital treats more than 250 000 children annually from those with life-threatening diseases to day-patients, many of whom are from marginalised communities. When RX Radio began broadcasting in November 2016 under the wing of the Red Cross Children’s Hospital, its aim was to to bring a little sunshine into these young lives, to put a smile on these children’s faces.

RX Radio is the brainchild of Dr Gabriel Urgoiti, RX Station Manager and Child Health Care Specialist at the hospital. “RX Radio has created a platform for children to voice their own issues and holding the mic gives them the power to engage not only with other children, but also with adults, asking questions and sharing their opinions,” says Urgoiti.

Pre-recorded and live shows are streamed via the internet 24/7. From music to podcasts and radio diaries, the station transmits audio and images through the hospital’s internal television system to all wards and public spaces.

“Children in the hospital form part of the show as they can request songs, dedications and live games by calling us or interacting through social media,” says Content Producer Noluyolo Ngomani. Our radio presenters are children as young as five and the oldest ones are 18. We also allow siblings of patients to co-host shows,” says Ngomani. “Those who are interested in becoming presenters attend a 5-day workshop where they learn about storytelling, radio reporting and production skills. We also send them out to live events where they interview people and come back to do a podcas.”

“The microphone gives them a voice; it changes the conversation around their illness and they are able to express what is going on deep inside themselves with their doctor and parents,” says Ngomani. “Their experience at the hospital becomes easier when they understand exactly what is wrong with them and how to cope.”


Further information:
“I have a muscle disorder so I can’t do lots of stuff, so I really like the radio.” Meet 10-year-old Naseerah du Toit. She presents her own weekly hour-long show with her sister, Yusrah, called Books and Breakfast. “When I started with the radio, I was very shy. Now I love it so much that I can talk for hours,” says Naseerah.

Naseerah suffers from a lifelong disease called Charcot-Marie-Tooth or CMT. Inherited from her father, the disease affects the nervous system causing a progressive weakening and loss of muscle tissue. This can make simple activities such as walking, brushing teeth or hair and getting dressed difficult. There is no cure for CMT and no medication to relieve the muscle pain. Physiotherapy is the only treatment to help Naseerah cope with her physical limitations. She has been in and out of the Red Cross Hospital for the last seven years. Radio RX has given her a platform to grow unhindered by the disability.

Their mother, Sukeena Sherry, is proud of how much her daughters have grown since they started their show last year. “Ngomani says they have what it takes and they are very professional even at their young age,” she says.

It, therefore, came as no surprise when the sisters were nominated for the Liberty Radio Awards in the internet radio category recently. “We were the youngest ever to be finalists, which was really exciting, and when we heard the news, I shouted: ‘Is it even true!’” says Yusrah.

Fifteen-year-old Talitha Counter is wheelchair-bound after contracting a viral infection at six weeks old. Since then, she has had limited movement in her upper body and depends on the help of a carer. Her treatment at the hospital involves regular physiotherapy to help strengthen her muscles.

Talitha’s positive attitude has helped her expand her mind and widen her world. RX Radio has provided a platform for her to interview specialists in many fields and talk about her journey and coming to terms with her disability.


But it is her love for music and dancing that lifts her spirits. “I sing a lot, and I also love dancing. See! (she shows her upper body move),” says Talitha. Due to her weak throat muscles, she is unable to clear her throat. She explains that this makes her voice sound unusual.

“I remember when she was just a little baby, she would cry and no tears would come out. It was then that I took her to hospital where she was in ICU. Later, they found out about her infection and what was wrong with her,” says Talitha’s mom, Yvonne. “I am grateful she has found the radio. It means a lot to her.”

Eleven-year-old Rowen Piorkowski was at death’s door four months ago when he contracted a rare form of leukemia; a cancer affecting 50 out of every million children. His mother, Julie, remembered the quick onset when he suddenly became very tired and bruised easily. The hospital administered intense chemotherapy treatment to fight the cancer progressively. “Rowan was in and out of the hospital all the time,” Julie explains. “Sometimes, we did not know if he would get better.”

Rowan used RX Radio to talk about his experience and learn about his condition. In interviews, he asks his oncologist questions about the illness. His mother takes part in the conversation, talking about her feelings. Rowan’s most recent show was at a nursing conference in Cape Town where he interviewed several of the speakers. “The radio experience has taught me to ask questions and talk to adults about stuff that we don’t normally do,” says Rowan.

Rowan is over the worst, for now, but needs to return to the hospital for regular tests. “I still go for regular check-ups, but I am now able to play my sport again as long as I am careful,” he says.

Seraj Bernards, 8, suffers from haemophilia, a hereditary condition affecting mainly males. Haemophilia impairs blood from clotting resulting in excessive bleeding, bruising and an increased risk of bleeding inside the joints or brain.

Seraj is one of the youngest presenters and loves talking about outdoor activity in his show. The microphone gives him the tool he needs to ask people about their physical experiences even though his own is severely limited. Haemophilia has also affected Seraj’s older brother, Hakeem, who was a regular presenter on RX Radio until recently, when he turned 18.

Our story:
This is a story of hope and wonder. The radio station has given children who live with disabilities the skills and tools to ask questions, to make their voices heard and to share their thoughts (and fears) with the world beyond their hospital beds.

Press Release:


RX Radio: Broadcasting for Children by Children
Eight to 18-year-olds behind a radio microphone, broadcasting live to children – and live-streaming to the world! It’s a world first for the Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital and a novel way for young patients and former patients to tell their own stories to peers who are still admitted to the hospital. Carte Blanche meets the award-winning young RX Radio’s broadcasters who say radio has a therapeutic effect that helps them deal with their chronic conditions and the healthcare they undergo, sometimes for years.
Producer: Annalise Lubbe
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


Script: RX Radio: Broadcasting for Children and by Children
Date: 16 May 2019
Duration: 9 Minutes

Link: The Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital in Cape Town treats thousands of children annually, some with life threatening diseases, but the patients here have found a unique way to share their stories.

Up sound: “Hi bookworms, first of all I am going to start off by telling you how my week went so far”

Up sound: In today’s traffic there are roadworks on the N1 inbound left …no delays”

Up sound: “The IEC will officially announce the results of the general elections….”

Up sound: “For the Rx Radio sports report, I am Runisha…..”

Up song….

Link: This is where the magic happens, RX Radio: the first radio station in the world presented by children for children live-streaming from a hospital broadcasting 24/7, from music, podcasts to radio diaries.

V/O The radio station is the brainchild of station manager Dr Gabriel Urgoiti, who has worked in child health care for 35 years. He has started two other community radio stations in Africa but working with these children brings unique benefits,

Dr. Gabriel Urgoiti: Station Manager: We started this radio station to provide children with the opportunity to have a safe platform so they can talk about things that are important to them.

V/O RX Radio went on air in 2016 transmitting audio and images through the hospital’s internal television system to all wards. It also livestreams on the internet and an easily downloadable App.

Dr. Gabriel Urgoiti: What makes this radio unique is that we are working with children that are sick, that are chronic patients in the hospital and have the most unbelievable, extraordinary life experiences.

Noluyolo Ngomani: Senior Content Producer: RX Radio - We broadcast 24/7 so programmes are generated by the children. They conceptualise their own shows, we just help them to be creative in this so we guide them in the scripting, research, running the desk.

V/O Children and their siblings who want to be presenters attend a workshop which introduces them to the world of radio and helps them get comfortable in the studio. With her radio and media training Noluyolo Ngomani helps them to find their voice.

UP sound: So welcome guys let’s do an ice breaker. up..uh ahlela, atiki tiki wasa”

V/O So far RX Radio has trained 83 reporters between the ages of 4 and 18.

Up audio Yolie: “so remember as a presenter you are telling a story when you are doing your show.

Up natural sound…

Talitha Counter: Presenter: I was always a shy person. Like when I started being on studio I always said my mom must not come because I am just not going to know what to say and what to do. Now I can say mommy you can stand there and you can watch me, I am not going to feel shy. It had given me self confidence.

V/O As a baby, 15 year old Talitha Counter, contracted Meningoencephalitis, an inflammation of the meninges and brain. She has never been able to walk and has limited use of her upper body. RX Radio has given her an opportunity to express herself.

Up sound: That was ...and now we are going to have an interview with Talitha.
Talitha: Good morning guys I am Talitha and I will be interviewing Gamuso regarding the RX Radio Newsletter. How was putting the newsletter together?
Guest: “it was amazing working with these kids…”

Talitha Counter: To be a presenter on Rx radio you need to be a good listener. You can't go in there all nervous because you are not going to know what to do and you are going to have a brain freeze because that is going to be a disaster.

Dr Gabriel Urgoiti: if you want to know what a child feels, or needs or knows, or wants, ask them and the radio station is providing them with that tool.

UP natural sound sequence:.…”I am Sumaya Mathews and I am twelve years old and I like to read and write and I also like stationary things….”
Hello I am Hakima Mathews, I am eight years old. I have a heart condition
Did you learn anything this week?
Yes.
What did you learn?
I forgot..

Up natural sound: Welcome to the show. How are you guys doing today?
Guest speaker: “Excited to be on the radio…..”

Dr. Gabriel Urgoiti: What is amazing is to see the fun and to see how this radio station is starting to contribute to the healing process of these kids.

Noluyolo Ngomani: Ultimately we are trying to make sure that the child here in this hospital doesn’t get lonely and they are having fun and be entertained while trying to deal with their condition.

Up natural sound…”I am Jesse, welcome back to Mama Africa by RX radio, by and for children…”

Claire Mawisa: So do you watch it as well. So you see them in the studio?

Child patient: “I see it and I listen the way they talk about how to save water, how to wash your hands…they tell sometimes stories”

Up natural sound Seraj: “in Durban it is sunny with a high of 24…”

V/O Eight-year-old Seraj Barends and his older brother, Hakeem, who is 18, suffer from haemophilia: a hereditary condition that impairs the blood’s ability to clot resulting in excessive bleeding and bruising.

Seraj Barends: Presenter RX Radio: The things I can’t do because of haemophilia; I cant play with these children outside, they are very rough.

Hakeem Barends: Presenter: RX Radio One for the biggest battles was I have a strong passion for soccer and haemophilia prevents me from playing.

Seraj Barends: My show is called “tackling the outdoors with Jesse”

Up sound: Hakeem: Seraj, what is your favourite outdoor activity?

Seraj Barends: “I actually like camping the most …”

Hakeem Barends: So the radio allows children to communicate with each other with same illnesses and even different ones. I am very fortunate that I am still able to move around and do things because I always felt it was unfair that I had this condition but when I walked into the cancer ward I can understand that I am better off than most.

V/O Two years ago twelve-year-old Rowan Piorkowski contracted acute myeloid leukemia. It’s a rare form of cancer that could be terminal. Only 50 out of every million children may get it.

Rowan Piorkowski: That was very bad. I felt nauseous all the time. So I got two scars right here. So I was very sick most of the stages but then I got better towards the end.

Claire Mawisa: Do you think it was a good experience for you to work here?

Rowen Piorkowski: Definitely. I had people that was sort of in the same situation as me and I
could talk to them about it and everybody like Wayne here and Chris and Gabs, they were all here to help me.

UP sound: So I am Rowen Piorkowski and I am a reporter for RX Radio and I will be interviewing CANSA’s Anthea-Lynn.

Claire Mawisa: How much power do the kids have at RX Radio?

Rowen Piorkowski: Well quite a lot because when you have your own show you start choosing who you want to interview and you write down your own script.

V/O Ten-year-old Naseerah du Toit has Charcot-Marie-Tooth or CMT, which affects the nervous system causing a weakening and loss of muscle tissue. Physiotherapy helps to manage the disease. Naseerah presents alongside her sister, Yusrah, who is 11.

Up sound: Yusrah: So I am super hungry. Naseerah how has your week been so far?
Naseerah: Well my week was hard and also a little boring”

Claire Mawisa: Was it scary for you when you started?

Naseerah du Toit: Presenter: RX Radio - Yes I was very scared and nervous. I never wanted to speak and then I got use to it and I then I decided to speak.

Claire Mawisa: What is your show about?

Yusrah du Toit: Presenter RX Radio: Our show is called Books and Breakfast with Yurah and Naseerah. It is aimed at getting young children to get them to love literature as much as I do.

Claire: What is your favourite thing about being a presenter on air?

Yusrah du Toit: My favourite part is generally just the speaking because I can speak forever whether it is live or recorded or vox pops or promos, I just love getting behind the mic.

Up sound…”as usual we have…sesame”

Noluyolo Ngomani: We were recently nominated for the Radio Liberty Awards so Yusrah’s Books and Breakfast which we produce got nominated for internet category and they got to be finalised, officially they did not win but we are proud of their achievement and I was inducted as the bright star.

Claire Mawisa: What was it like being nominated for an award?

Yusrah du Toit: We were the youngest ever to be nominated. All of the other nominees were actually adults, so I think is a very big deal.

Up sound:...”and if you are here in the hospital you can listen on channel 10”

Dr Gabriel Urgoiti: The dream is very simple to reach every single hospital with a paediatric ward in South Africa.

Talitha up song...

Talitha Counter: I would like to say to the kids that if they have dreams they must not give up on their dreams. Follow your heart wherever, just conquer them. Be good and peace out.

Up sound…”it is the second...and we have got some great interviews”

END

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We hear the young voices behind the microphone of the first radio station in the world to live-stream from a children’s hospital: presented by children they share their life stories.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: RX Radio at the Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital in Cape Town is presented by children who share their stories of hope and understanding their chronic health conditions they live with. Talking about their experiences in hospital helps them to cope better and teaches them valuable life skills.
metadata.Summary: The Red Cross War Memorial Children’s Hospital is dedicated entirely to children. The hospital treats more than 250 000 children annually from those with life-threatening diseases to day-patients, many of whom are from marginalised communities. When RX Radio began broadcasting in November 2016 under the wing of the Red Cross Children’s Hospital, its aim was to to bring a little sunshine into these young lives, to put a smile on these children’s faces. RX Radio is the brainchild of Dr Gabriel Urgoiti, RX Station Manager and Child Health Care Specialist at the hospital. “RX Radio has created a platform for children to voice their own issues and holding the mic gives them the power to engage not only with other children, but also with adults, asking questions and sharing their opinions,” says Urgoiti. Pre-recorded and live shows are streamed via the internet 24/7. From music to podcasts and radio diaries, the station transmits audio and images through the hospital’s internal television system to all wards and public spaces. “Children in the hospital form part of the show as they can request songs, dedications and live games by calling us or interacting through social media,” says Content Producer Noluyolo Ngomani. Our radio presenters are children as young as five and the oldest ones are 18. We also allow siblings of patients to co-host shows,” says Ngomani. “Those who are interested in becoming presenters attend a 5-day workshop where they learn about storytelling, radio reporting and production skills. We also send them out to live events where they interview people and come back to do a podcas.” “The microphone gives them a voice; it changes the conversation around their illness and they are able to express what is going on deep inside themselves with their doctor and parents,” says Ngomani. “Their experience at the hospital becomes easier when they understand exactly what is wrong with them and how to cope.”
metadata.Further information: “I have a muscle disorder so I can’t do lots of stuff, so I really like the radio.” Meet 10-year-old Naseerah du Toit. She presents her own weekly hour-long show with her sister, Yusrah, called Books and Breakfast. “When I started with the radio, I was very shy. Now I love it so much that I can talk for hours,” says Naseerah. Naseerah suffers from a lifelong disease called Charcot-Marie-Tooth or CMT. Inherited from her father, the disease affects the nervous system causing a progressive weakening and loss of muscle tissue. This can make simple activities such as walking, brushing teeth or hair and getting dressed difficult. There is no cure for CMT and no medication to relieve the muscle pain. Physiotherapy is the only treatment to help Naseerah cope with her physical limitations. She has been in and out of the Red Cross Hospital for the last seven years. Radio RX has given her a platform to grow unhindered by the disability. Their mother, Sukeena Sherry, is proud of how much her daughters have grown since they started their show last year. “Ngomani says they have what it takes and they are very professional even at their young age,” she says. It, therefore, came as no surprise when the sisters were nominated for the Liberty Radio Awards in the internet radio category recently. “We were the youngest ever to be finalists, which was really exciting, and when we heard the news, I shouted: ‘Is it even true!’” says Yusrah. Fifteen-year-old Talitha Counter is wheelchair-bound after contracting a viral infection at six weeks old. Since then, she has had limited movement in her upper body and depends on the help of a carer. Her treatment at the hospital involves regular physiotherapy to help strengthen her muscles. Talitha’s positive attitude has helped her expand her mind and widen her world. RX Radio has provided a platform for her to interview specialists in many fields and talk about her journey and coming to terms with her disability. But it is her love for music and dancing that lifts her spirits. “I sing a lot, and I also love dancing. See! (she shows her upper body move),” says Talitha. Due to her weak throat muscles, she is unable to clear her throat. She explains that this makes her voice sound unusual. “I remember when she was just a little baby, she would cry and no tears would come out. It was then that I took her to hospital where she was in ICU. Later, they found out about her infection and what was wrong with her,” says Talitha’s mom, Yvonne. “I am grateful she has found the radio. It means a lot to her.” Eleven-year-old Rowen Piorkowski was at death’s door four months ago when he contracted a rare form of leukemia; a cancer affecting 50 out of every million children. His mother, Julie, remembered the quick onset when he suddenly became very tired and bruised easily. The hospital administered intense chemotherapy treatment to fight the cancer progressively. “Rowan was in and out of the hospital all the time,” Julie explains. “Sometimes, we did not know if he would get better.” Rowan used RX Radio to talk about his experience and learn about his condition. In interviews, he asks his oncologist questions about the illness. His mother takes part in the conversation, talking about her feelings. Rowan’s most recent show was at a nursing conference in Cape Town where he interviewed several of the speakers. “The radio experience has taught me to ask questions and talk to adults about stuff that we don’t normally do,” says Rowan. Rowan is over the worst, for now, but needs to return to the hospital for regular tests. “I still go for regular check-ups, but I am now able to play my sport again as long as I am careful,” he says. Seraj Bernards, 8, suffers from haemophilia, a hereditary condition affecting mainly males. Haemophilia impairs blood from clotting resulting in excessive bleeding, bruising and an increased risk of bleeding inside the joints or brain. Seraj is one of the youngest presenters and loves talking about outdoor activity in his show. The microphone gives him the tool he needs to ask people about their physical experiences even though his own is severely limited. Haemophilia has also affected Seraj’s older brother, Hakeem, who was a regular presenter on RX Radio until recently, when he turned 18. Our story: This is a story of hope and wonder. The radio station has given children who live with disabilities the skills and tools to ask questions, to make their voices heard and to share their thoughts (and fears) with the world beyond their hospital beds.
